intro: A painted animal, a textile and a suspended metal surface offer three different ways to build a lively picture from repeated elements.
alt: Microsoft views a colorful animal painting, a rhythmic textile study and a large hanging made of linked colored metal.

variants.name: Tinga Tinga
variants.look: Bright enamel color and bold contours frame the animal against repeating leaves.
variants.history: Edward Saidi Tingatinga developed a practice in Dar es Salaam in the late 1960s. Relatives and other painters carried it forward in new directions.
variants.when: Study it when bold silhouettes and pattern need to fill a scene with energy.
variants.why: Opaque color keeps every shape distinct and makes repetition easy to see.

variants.name: Oshogbo School
variants.look: Plants and animal-like shapes bend in repeated arcs across the textile study.
variants.history: Workshops that grew around Mbari Mbayo in 1960s Oshogbo, now also spelled Osogbo, brought artists together across print, textile, painting and performance.
variants.when: Study the workshops as a way to understand how artists develop individually through shared experimentation.
variants.why: A familiar design can change character when its line moves to cloth, paint or another medium.

source.label: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art

variants.name: El Anatsui-style metal tapestry
variants.look: Hundreds of small reflective pieces take on the flow and folds of a hanging cloth.
variants.history: El Anatsui, born in Ghana and long based in Nigeria, developed large flexible works from linked aluminum liquor-bottle material and copper wire.
variants.when: Study the artist's work when considering what happens to used material at radically different scales.
variants.why: Near the surface each piece has its own history and sheen. Across a room the pieces read as one field.

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly 3 equally wide scenes side by side in stated order in a wide 3:1 montage, separations only at vertical boundaries. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space. Scene list in exact order: Tanzania Tinga Tinga playful enamel study of an elephant under patterned leaves and bright solid color, bold contours; Nigerian Oshogbo workshop-inspired study, rhythmic curving plant and animal shapes in deep dye colors on textile; El Anatsui-inspired process study showing a hanging cloth-like surface assembled from hundreds of differently-colored folded metal pieces connected with copper wire, a small process sample with distinct red-gold-silver geometry, not a copy of an artwork. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
